posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-value CRO post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the compliance pain around unexplainable AI output, add the 'auditability gap' insight without pitching
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' answer is going to end careers before it ends the AI trend. The real issue isn't accuracy — it's that most AI tools produce a result with no visible working. Finance and compliance teams don't just need the right number, they need the trail that leads to it. How many analytics tools today can actually hand you that?

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person consultancy hit the classic adoption wall — validate that trust is the real product, not the dashboard
posts.draft_comment: 18 months is actually pretty normal for this — the dashboard was never the problem. Finance teams have been burned by numbers that looked right but weren't, so Excel feels safer because at least they know where the mistakes live. The real work is building enough of a track record that someone's willing to stake their reputation on a number they didn't personally pull. How many times did the dashboard have to be wrong before they stopped checking it?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging on dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why nobody looks' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is basically a way of saying 'we don't know what matters yet.' The jump to 85% usage tells you everything — people don't avoid dashboards because they're lazy, they avoid them because they've learned the dashboard won't help them make a call. The real question is who had the authority to delete 42 metrics, because that fight is usually harder than building the thing in the first place.

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging on self-service BI chaos — validate the 'who owns truth' framing, add the insight that the tooling problem is actually a governance problem in disguise
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports thing is so familiar it hurts. Everyone gets access, nobody gets alignment — and then three months later the data team is firefighting trust, not building anything. The real issue isn't self-service vs centralised, it's that most orgs handed out the keys before they'd agreed what the car was for. What does 'revenue' mean at Velocity — is that even written down somewhere?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO framing AI hallucinations as a security risk — validate the reframe, add the specific analytics angle that makes it concrete, with a CEO prospect watching
posts.draft_comment: The security framing is exactly right and I think it's underused. A hallucinated user input gets caught by validation layers — a hallucinated revenue figure in an AI-generated report goes straight into a board deck with nobody checking it. The trust model is completely backwards. Who in your org is actually responsible when that number gets quoted to an auditor?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with a post about BI tools failing business users — validate the core frustration with a specific observation, add the hidden reason why it happens
posts.draft_comment: That £200k number is brutal, but honestly the price isn't even the worst part — it's the 6 months of internal goodwill burned trying to get people to use it. The dirty secret is most BI tools are still designed around the person querying the data, not the person who just needs an answer on a Tuesday morning. So the 'self-service' is real, it's just self-service for analysts. What would it actually take for a 50-person company to call a BI tool genuinely useful — not impressive, just useful?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a likely ICP company surfacing a classic data trust problem — validate the cultural root cause, add the layer about why tooling gets blamed first
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, one dataset, three answers — that's not a filter problem, that's a 'who owns the truth' problem. And the reason everyone points at the BI tool is because it's easier to blame software than to have the governance conversation. The CFO probably still doesn't fully trust the dashboard even after you explained it. Does anyone ever really?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing a real adoption failure pattern — validate the 'nobody knows what to ask' insight and reframe it as a data literacy problem, not a tooling problem
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number doesn't surprise me at all. The gap isn't Copilot vs ChatGPT — it's that most people don't have a clear enough mental model of their own data to know what questions are even worth asking. Shadow AI feels like freedom but it's usually just faster guessing. What does the 12% who stuck with it actually have in common?
